abstract: Free-living unicellular organisms known as ciliates rely on fluid flows to perform essential functions. These flows emerge from the coordinated activity of thousands of cilia organized into arrays with highly diverse architectures. Within a species, the structure of the ciliary array is highly stereotyped and persists in time, raising the question of how a single cell achieves multiple distinct flow functions from one fixed array architecture. Here, we investigate how the ciliary array in the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia enables this organism to feed and swim simultaneously. Using expansion microscopy and high-speed imaging, we measure ciliary organization and kinematics, from individual beat dynamics to collective metachronal wave patterns, together with the flows these cilia generate. We find that the cell's surface is partitioned into domains with distinct spatiotemporal cilia organization. In addition to the oral apparatus, there are two structurally different domains. One is a densely ciliated, high-frequency beating domain located anterior to the oral apparatus, and the other covers the remainder of the cell's surface, where cilia are more sparsely distributed and slower-beating. Selective removal of each results in impaired feeding or swimming, respectively, demonstrating that each domain is functionally specialized. Our work establishes heterogeneity in spatiotemporal ciliary patterning as a mechanism that allows a single cell to generate multiple flow functions. By measuring cilia organization and the flows they generate, we uncover general physical principles by which cilia arrays produce flow patterns that underlie diverse biological functions.
